title: Show HN: Browsentic Open-source Claude for Chrome alternative for any agent CLI
body:
A personal agent harness lives in your existing browser, connects to your claude-code (or any other major harness codex or cursor-cli...) NOT the SDK API, exposes web-optimized tools to the harness - that's Browsentic.
A free, opensource (Apache 2.0) with rich capabilities alternative to Comet, BrowserOS, Browser-use, Claude for Chrome or nanobrowser.
The unique architecture of Browsentic makes it different from all other alternatives. It uses a loopback MCP server that spawns claude/codex/OpenCode/Cursor harness in a detached process. You can already guess, it is a bi-directional MCP, you can browse agentic through the browser harness or through any MCP client.
Browsentic doesn't require any new browser to install and not limited to chromium, it supports Firefox as well. By default you don't even need CDP to perform core agentic browsing.
Capabilities: core accessibilities (50+ compare to nanobrowser only had 20), custom skill, record-replay, schedule-monitoring-notification, resolves captcha autonomously, has it's own memory, voice orb over web-speech API, can sideload custom tools, platform + browser + agent agnostic
It is opensource, no API key, no telemetry & local first and actively maintained and yesterday was the first public stable launch (v0.8.0)
Currently I'm the only author but every & any contribution or suggestion will be more than welcome :)
Source: https://github.com/imshaikot/browsentic
Install guide: https://browsentic.com/install
Docs: https://browsentic.com/docs
Install video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o8t4l9Q9BkE

title: Comment on: Tell HN: Bob Cringely has died
body:
I don't really understand what your comment is trying to say, but I read through the last few pages of his blog and all the posts after the first one from 2026 announcing his return seem AI generated. I think it's a shame, as I loved his writing style in "Accidental Empires" and in his earlier blog posts and columns. It's strange to me that someone who had spent most of his life writing either didn't notice or didn't care about the drop in quality from using LLMs to write.
> Look at his last few blog posts, outlining a radical alternative to LLMs. Read closely, and at the heart of that idea we find "assume enterprise search".
I found the patent for his company's technology (https://patents.google.com/patent/US20250259069A1). I always have trouble reading patents, but as far as I can tell it's basically a wrapper around commodity LLMs. The reliability improvements come from prompting the LLM to only source its data from an external database that you provide rather than from whatever it was trained on, and from prompting multiple LLMs simultaneously then doing semantic analysis on the responses to make sure they all agree. I imagine that doing this would probably reduce hallucinations, but there's no hard constraint to prevent them entirely and I'm not sure what the moat is.

title: Comment on: In Ukraine, distributed renewables foil Russia's assaults
body:
I am not sure if solar panel are worth using in places where the sky is clear only several months a year. A desert (for example, in Africa or Emirates) would be a better place for them.
Wouldn't it be better to have thousands of traditional natural gas, coal or diesel-powered generators to replace large centralized plants? They are compact (easier to hide). A 2 MW generator is a size of a truck. And portable 24 MW generator is a size of several trucks. Before the war, they had ~44 GW of generation (~1 kW per person), so one needs thousands of mobile generators to replace the system, and I doubt anyone provided them.
I wish there was a comparison of installation costs and generation costs for traditional and renewable energy. Without comparison, it might be that renewables are simply not worth investing yet.
One company advertises solar panels [1] and claims that 1 MW scale array requires 3000 panels and costs over $1M. While used diesel-powered 2MW generator costs several hundreds thousands USD. Why would someone buy one array when for that price several diesel generators can be bought?
Traditional energy is cheap. For example, Russia has 240 GW of generation, almost no solar and wind, and electricity costs 8 cents per kWh and in the West the energy is super expensive despite using solar and wind power. Also, diesel costs 65 RUB/liter, or 2.94 USD/US gallon (if 1 US gallon = 3.78 L) and again in the West for some reason it is overpriced. Maybe the renewables are only profitable with overpriced natural resources and government subsidies, without a comparison it is difficult to say.
[1] https://solartechonline.com/blog/what-is-a-solar-array/

title: Comment on: The evolution of effective altruism
body:
That's how I understand it: a movement encouraging people to donate their wealth to good causes which save and improve lives.
However, there's some who predict an existential future risk such as an AI apocalypse. If that's the case, why save a child's life today when we'll all be killed by AI tomorrow? Critics would call this funding pet projects rather than altruism.
But you can even further down this line of thinking. If you're a billionaire and see yourself as the only hope of saving humanity from extinction, why donate any of your wealth? You should be doing the opposite, gathering as much wealth and power as possible. Taxes and laws that get in your way are impediments to the salvation of humanity.
I'm pretty sure most of the criticism is for folks in the latter groups. I wish there were different words to distinguish them better, because I like the idea of encouraging charity but somehow a handful of billionaires have poisoned the word altruism.

title: Comment on: Anatomy of a Lean proof for software engineers
body:
You only need to trust your spec and the Lean kernel. If you trust those two things, you don't ever need to manually inspect or check the proof. That's the job of the Lean kernel, and your trust of it transfers over to trust of any proof verified by it.
Making sure your spec is correct -- and that it's expressed at a level of abstraction that both captures what matters, without overly constraining implementation details within the repo -- is the hard part. The more the spec constrains implementation details, the less you can ask an agent to, e.g., try many ideas to optimize a specific component without breaking correctness. And of course if the spec isn't enforcing what you wanted it to, then all the proofs don't count for much.
Some people say the spec issues are enough reason to avoid formal methods, but I'm not convinced. Part of me truly thinks AI formal methods is the future of a lot of software engineering. The basis of that belief for me is that the industry has collectively put almost no effort yet into solving the spec problem, and that's because for decades formal methods were too expensive to seriously consider most of the time. Now that AI is fundamentally shifting the economics, there's now, for the first time ever, a real incentive to try to solve the spec problem. And frankly it seems solvable to me; I view it as more of a product design and UI problem than a purely technical one.

title: Comment on: How to scale intent, quality, and artistry with AI [video]
body:
The problem isn't that you can't use AI to uplevel your creativity. It's that doing it slows you down, so you end up at a marked disadvantage, because others who just prompt "hey Claude, make me X" will produce 100 good enough slop-pieces in the time it takes you to finish one.
For the vast majority of paying customers or social media appreciators, that low-effort slop is sufficient. It's cheap, fast, and gets better with every passing month. So if your overriding goal is to scale to win in that marketplace, then you can only scale by giving up on quality and artistry. It's a race to the bottom.
I think the only way to win is to push back on the notion that you need to work on superhuman scale in the first place. You can differentiate yourself from AI by asserting you're human and that there's inherent value in human art. You'll find some customers willing to pay extra for that, just like some hire a woodworker instead of buying at Ikea. But it's going to be a tough market for artisans because fewer and fewer people are forced to buy the fruits of your intellectual labor.
In software engineering specifically, we gleefully decided that speed and cost are the only thing that matters and we celebrate "hey Claude, make me X" projects the same as we celebrate human ingenuity (case in point: HN front page). So for SWEs, even that "I'm a human" route may be unavailable.

title: Comment on: So you think you could be an electrician?
body:
I read a book called "Nothing to Envy: Ordinary Lives in North Korea" by Barbara Demick, about North Koreans in the 1990s that escaped into China and told their story. One of the interesting parts of it is about the planned economy, and all the control the government exerts over the economy in NK.
There was a massive famine I didn't know about in the mid-to-late 1990s in NK, and millions died. During this period, an underground capitalism took over, where people were producing food in various ways, often grown in their own gardens, and then buying and selling from each other, with barter rates / prices determined by availability.
While I agree with you that countries can make rules that fix prices (or do whatever they want), there is an underlying set of mechanisms to supply and demand that are not derived from law, but logic. If I have 5 cupcakes, and there are 100 people that want them, unless someone points a gun at me and says "Sell them each for 5 cents" (while the 100 people all fight over who gets to pay), the natural incentive structure would essentially be an auction to figure out who is willing to pay the most, and then sell it to them. That's not some legal theory or set of laws, but rather the human condition.
Of course, it doesn't play out this way in reality. In reality, it all comes down to power, and those with power take whatever they want, but my point here is that supply and demand exist outside of a legal structure, and if there's only one electrician, and there's enough work for 10 electricians, that one electrician can server the richest 1/10 of those in need (and charge accordingly to select that 1/10), and it is rational to do so independent of any laws made. So much so, in fact, that laws are advisory, but the fundamental incentives are inherent.
This is why I like incentives more than rules: they're less brittle.

title: Show HN: Build with Python – a beginner course where your code draws
body:
Hi HN, I built this because I watched my daughter struggle at learning Python. I made something that runs only in the browser with visuals rather than relying on CLI/terminal output. No need to worry about python installation, package versions, venv etc.
The lab runs with Pyodide in a web worker, and the program output is a picture by the side of the code block. A user would experiment with the code, and see the immediate changes in the visual output.
The course has 13 modules, with the first 6 foundation modules free, module 7-13 with free readings but guide labs for a one-time price of $49.
Please give it a try at https://scimigo.com/en/learn/build-with-python
Send me feedback on the UX and on the exercise design, especially if you teach kids to program.
I am also working on a C++ version for beginners (also with browser, no gcc or command lines). stay tuned.

title: [early engagement] NHS England: Curated literature based database of germline human genomic variants database
body:
The requirement is for a database or a tool that clinicians can use to search for rare inherited disease mutations, or search for an overview of known mutations associated with a particular disease, interpreting clinical test results, looking for the likely causal mutation in a list of variants, or seeking to integrate mutation content into your custom NGS pipeline or data repository.

body:

title: [early engagement] Cabinet Office: National School of Government and Public Services
body:
Cabinet Office intends to procure a robust, industry-standard Software as a Service (SaaS) Learning Management System (LMS) through the Government Commercial Agency's (GCA) RM6219 Learning and Training Dynamic Purchasing System (DPS), to support the new National School of Government and Public Services Learning & Development (L&D) offering.
The LMS will provide a scalable platform to support a user base of over 558,000 users and must meet mandatory security and information assurance requirements, including UK hosting of data and adherence to Secure by Design principles.
Mandatory Requirements
Security and information assurance requirements, specifically mandatory UK hosting of data and adherence to 'Secure by Design' requirements
Scalable and accessible to support over 558,000 users
Please note - The mandatory requirement must be met by all potential bidders
Essential requirements
Core LMS capability (i.e. learning catalogue, content tagging) 
Booking and administration functionality
Admin controls for end-to-end of central delivery offer and repository
Migration support (for catalogue of learning)
Quality data, including feedback, reporting and evaluation 
The requirement is for the provision of the LMS platform and associated implementation/support services. L&D content supplied by the LMS provider is out of scope; the platform will be used to host internally developed learning content.
